Stablecoin legislation has been drafted in Congress I read the bill. TL;DR decentralized stables become illegal in the US (DAI, LUSD, RAI, etc. become illegal🚨) while centralized stables, defi, Ethereum, and ETH win big. High-level summary⬇️ - decentralized stables become illegal in the US. DAI, LUSD, RAI etc. - foreign stables become illegal in the US. National boundaries for stables - imo ETH sees significant uptake as a payment method that's both legal and decentralized - licensed stables, eg. USDC, become huge winners and permitted to access Fed accounts directly Full summary⬇️ 1. The Act makes it illegal to offer unlicensed stablecoins in the US, with a maximum fine of $1M and of 5 years in prison. The Act is specific that this applies globally. Their definition of "stablecoin" is very broad and includes DAI, LUSD, floating stables like RAI, and even includes exotic quasi-stables as long as they are designed to be redeemable for a relatively fixed amount of "monetary value", including all fiat currencies. For example, this act makes it illegal to build DAI in America, illegal to send DAI to an American business or person living in the US, and illegal for foreign-licensed or unlicensed stablecoins to be offered to Americans in any way. Essentially, this bill draws national borders around stables by making decentralized stables and foreign-licensed stables illegal in America. imo the illegalization of unlicensed and foreign stables seems likely to greatly benefit the uptake of non-stable payment tokens, especially ETH. 2. The Act makes the stablecoin licensing process structured but ultimately discretionary. They decide who gets to issue licensed stables. 3. Allows stables to be collateralized by insured deposits in some cases. Could perhaps cause deposit tokens to fall under this regulation as "stablecoins backed by bank deposits". 4. Gives stable operators direct access to the Federal Reserve. Eg. Circle could have accounts at the Fed. 5. Launches an official study on a CBDC. Includes a surprisingly thoughtful list of criteria to study, including the potential impact of a CBDC on the competitive landscape of stablecoins. 6. The Act defines "payment system" broadly in a way that, imo, would include many wallets, bridges, defi, and crypto payment apps. But, the Act does not regulate these payment systems. They aren't banning or licensing defi in this Act. I'm not a lawyer, and this was my best-effort interpretation of the Act. Ethereum is NOT a protocol, you know things like TCP/IP and HTTP. The crypto world is in a mass psychosis. VC funds have blossomed on the thesis that L1s are “protocols” for finance. Nope, these are language and compute environments. ETH was the first language to gain popularity for DeFi apps. But it was created before we knew what DeFi needs were. We have seen this before… COBOL, Fortran, Lisp, C, JS, Rust. Each language builds from learnings of the past and upon the needs of new domains. Old languages continue to be used, but many wane, while new languages come and gain adoption. ETH’s Solidity is like COBOL, early and unlikely to be matched for future needs. To be clear: - a PROTOCOL is a simple standard for MESSAGING - a LANGUAGE is a complex standard for COMPUTE The former has longer and stronger network effects, while the latter tends to fade over time to new challengers. Bitcoin is more of the former while Ethereum is more like the latter. Like COBOL it’s quite unlikely Solidity will be what we build DeFi apps on in say 10+ years. If you think it will evolve over time to compete, remember blockchains are very hard to upgrade. In other words, don't believe the VC hype that these are protocols like TCP/IP that has long term winners, expect stiff competition in L1 networks, it's unlikely they will gain long term increasing dominance over the long arc.

Why Ordinals? Why NFTs on Bitcoin? Just... WHY? We’ve had NFTs on Ethereum for a long time. Ethereum has sophisticated smart contracts. Ethereum has far more functionality. Ethereum has the ability to store things on-chain, and with as much effective immutability as Bitcoin, insofar as you believe Ethereum will exist for as long as Bitcoin. ..and perhaps therein lies the detail. Blockchains can be thought of as canvases (or.. layers), on top of which you can do things. You can store a public record of ownership, and that ownership may represent a digital currency, or, it may represent something else. Like... Art. An Ordinals OG and level headed thinker, @dazza9x, wrote this great tweet sharing his thesis: https://twitter.com/dazza9x/status/1671081649063481346. And that reminded me of this tweet from a week or two back by @DeeZe, on one of the “issues” with collecting on Tezos: https://twitter.com/DeeZe/status/1670377749096038402. The art is AMAZING, but if there is less confidence in the chain, it might deter some collectoooors. Both tweets hit home to me, and put together, make a lot of sense. It’s also a concern a lot of people have had for collecting on Cardano, Solana, Avalanche, or one of many other chains that are widely viewed as less likely to exist / be thriving in a decade or five in comparison to Ethereum. We actually saw the reality of Solana’s centralization issue implode and the impact that had on the entire ecosystem after FTX’s collapse. Chain-risk is a real thought/concern when collecting NFTs, and especially when investing in them. And you can yell at me until you’re blue in the face about collecting art for art’s sake, but the reality is the vast vast vast majority of collectors also consider the financial elements and ability to re-sell their jpegs at some point for profit, even if they’re truly okay with things going to zero. None of us have unlimited monies. And even if you do purely only care about the art, you should care about it existing and being recoverable decades from now. SO. If the risk increases when moving from Ethereum to most other chains, would it not stand to reason that the risk reduces when moving to Bitcoin, (un?)arguably the most decentralized, secure, and likely-to-exist chain a century from now? This, to me, is the core thesis and WHY that collecting on Bitcoin might make sense. It is through this lens that I view Ordinals, and have since February, even if I haven’t been active in the ecosystem until recently. The Drawbacks Ordinals are not some holy grail solution to NFTs. Much of the power of NFTs is due to smart contracts and the interoperability possible between a decentralized web of tokens. The ability to transact at speed and scale is also an important element for a large percentage of NFTs, and neither is particularly feasible on Bitcoin (at the L1 layer at least). Energy consumption was / is an enormous narrative around Blockchain technology and many people, companies, and governments will have a much easier time justifying transacting on Ethereum or another PoS chain vs a PoW one. For some, Bitcoin is not “meant” to serve as a blockchain for jpegs, or any utility beyond being a digital currency. It muddies the water. The thesis and bull case for Bitcoin was/is clear without Ordinals: digital gold. Scarce, secure, decentralized. Or as Satoshi famously and eloquently put it: A purely peer-to-peer version of electronic cash would allow online payments to be sent directly from one party to another without going through a financial institution. Debating this last point is probably beyond the scope of what I want to cover today, but it would be remiss to not at least mention it. Not all fans of Bitcoin are fans of Ordinals. Then again, not all fans of Ethereum were/are fans of NFTs. Who knows where this all goes but it's a fun area to be exploring, and I have to say, the community is genuinely wonderful and full of great humans. Perhaps because of a shared trait that generally great humans share: curiosity. p.s if you share that curiosity, drop a note below - I am looking to invite people wanting to learn and explore ordinals into our Discord server, so we can all help each other navigate this space together. Sensibly.

ERC-6551 & The Future of NFTs Recently there was a MASSIVE improvement to the entire Ethereum NFT ecosystem and very few people are talking about it ..at least relative to the amount of attention being given to the latest Azuki or Yuga or Ether FUD. So I want to talk about it. Because it's Really. Freaking. Cool. What is ERC-6551? At a high level, ERC-6551 (also known as Token Bound Accounts) makes it possible for NFTs to have their own wallet. Rather than a person owning assets, the token itself can hold custody of the assets. Basically: every NFT can now own / store within it ETH as well as ERC-721, 1155, and 20 tokens. Actually an NFT can store an NFT which itself stores other NFTs. It’s NFTs all the way down. How? The gist of it is that there is an on-chain and permissionless Registry (a smart contract) which can be used by anyone to create token bound accounts and deploy them for any NFTs. The beauty of this is that it’s backwards compatible, so all existing NFTs are able to hold tokens. Honestly it’s a technological marvel that they were able to do this. You don’t need to wrap tokens, upgrade contracts, etc. It just.. works. Actually, all NFTs already have their own accounts. If you own NFTs.. those NFTs have their own accounts. Why? It’s always good to ask WHY — why might we want NFTs to custody assets? What are the use cases? How does this make the future better? The first thing that came to mind to me was airdrops. Instead of projects taking snapshots and airdropping tokens to the holders of NFTs, they can airdrop them directly to the NFTs themselves. Think about that for a moment. This eliminates the need for all the pre-snapshot/post-snapshot kerfuffling about. No more immediately flooring the collection after the snapshot. The airdrop goes directly to the NFT, and everyone can see clearly on-chain the assets held within that NFT. But there are lots of other ways ERC-6551 makes a lot of sense too. Think about playing a game and owning your character. The TRUTH about HEX; Where did the ETH go??? On December 2, 2019, Richard Heart launched HEX on the Ethereum blockchain, not as a work-in-progress but as a finalized, immutable contract. Void of any admin keys, this meant no changes could be instigated post-launch. Hex was marketed as the first high interest blockchain certificate of deposit. For those eager to own the HEX token, two primary avenues beckoned: 1. Bitcoin Free Claim: Bitcoin owners were given a unique advantage. By authenticating ownership of a Bitcoin wallet, they could clinch up to 13,000 HEX for every Bitcoin they possessed. 2. Adoption Amplifier (AA): The AA lobby was open for HEX's first 351 days. Enthusiasts could send ETH, and at the day's end, mint their HEX share relative to their ETH contribution. For instance, if you contributed 1 ETH out of a 100 ETH pot, you'd be entitled to 1% of that day's HEX. In the first day of the AA, 1 billion Hex were available in the AA lobby. Around 510 million HEX were available each day after that until the AA phase concluded on Big Pay Day. Although the rules for transforming ETH into HEX were simple, a resonating question emerged: "Where does the ETH go?" Richard remained elusive on this, neither confirming nor denying if the ETH would enrich him or boost HEX's outreach. Most, including me, speculated that the ETH probably lined Richard's pockets. But in essence, the destination and utility of the ETH was moot. HEX, being a completed product, required no additional development. Users minted HEX, not by buying but by “Transforming” ETH as stipulated by the contract. Less than two weeks after the first HEX tokens were minted by users, the HEX/ETH liquidity pair was added to Uniswap V1, serving as a third conduit to acquire HEX. Although Uniswap was relatively nascent at the time, it swiftly became a HEX hub. The platform's real-time pricing and immediate HEX procurement, sans the AA lobby's suspense, made it a favorite. With this new accessibility to HEX, arbitrage opportunities burgeoned. Astute users observed that if the AA transformation rate surpassed Uniswap's swap rate, they could swap HEX for ETH just as the AA lobby was sealing and subsequently mint more HEX than they started with. Conversely, one could channel ETH to the AA, mint HEX, and then offload the HEX for a greater ETH amount. Both of these arbitrage plays would significantly suppress the price. For whoever controlled the Flush Address, a conundrum was evident: - Should they allow individuals to capitalize on the AA/Uniswap arbitrage, causing immense sell pressure and depressing HEX’s value? - Or should they orchestrate the cyclical repurposing of ETH, stymieing arbitrage, but increase the centralization of HEX ownership? Now, what is the HEX Flush Address??? This address had the unique capability to extract any ETH routed to the AA. Beginning around HEX's integration on Uniswap, substantial ETH inflows into the AA, often just moments before the day ended, were noticeable. Strikingly, the HEX procured from these late-stage contributions were not being sold. Simultaneously, ETH from the flush address seemed to dance between various individual addresses and major exchanges such as Bybit and Binance. This rhythmic transfer led to suspicions that Richard might be cyclically reintroducing ETH into the AA, effectively pocketing HEX without any real expenditure. While not irrefutably confirmed, the theory holds water. The maze of HEX's journey brings to light a compelling argument: that the suspected act of recycling ETH was indeed a safeguard rather than a detriment to other HEX holders. Such an approach, if viewed holistically, emerged as a lesser evil in a scenario where unchecked arbitrage could have debilitated HEX's value. Moreover, any deliberate opacity concerning the control of the Flush Address or the intended utility of the ETH wasn't arbitrary or misleading. Instead, it was a strategic measure to ensure non-violation of securities laws as perceived by Richard Heart. The intricate tapestry of such decisions, strategies, and actions is what endears Richard to the passionate Hexican community. Conversely, it's these very threads of complexity that lead to misinterpretations by a larger audience. The quintessential dichotomy of Richard Heart's approach to HEX represents the chasm between those who delve deep into understanding the nuances and those who form judgments from a distance in the vast world of crypto. I will make this even easier for you all. 👇 CRYPTOPUNKS. Launched in June 2017 by Larva Labs, Cryptopunks were originally free for anyone with an Ethereum wallet to claim (+ gas). The Punks were a huge hit at launch and all of them were claimed incredibly fast. In the original Cryptopunks smart contract, there was a code error that caused Ethereum to be allocated to the buyer instead of the seller when a purchase was made. In other words, a buyer was immediately refunded for their purchase and was able to keep the Punk. Not long after the bug was found a newer version of the Punks contract (Version 2, V2) was released and Punks were airdropped to this new contract. V1 Punk owners are now able to wrap their Punks into an ERC-721 contract (another kind of standardized smart contract) and patch over the bug. This recovery of the original Punks smart contract is a community led and rapidly growing phenomenon consisting of original Punk claimant’s, NFT historians, digital archeologists and extremely talented developers. There is no clear leader and all important decisions are voted on by community members. V1 Punks exist just as V2s do. This cannot be changed or undone since the V1 Punks are a permanent part of the blockchain. The new wrappers impart a slight change to the image in the form of a new background While this is a very modest change in the image, the core Punk remains the same. While the V1 Punks still exist in their original form, so does the existing bug in the V1 contract so NEVER put an unwrapped V1 on sale as you will most likely loose it. V1 Punks are not a derivative but are in fact the "original/classic" Cryptopunks. This is verified on the Ethereum blockchain and is immutable.

9 takeaways, devconnect istanbul: 1. @ethereum has all but crushed the alt-L1 thesis at this point, with two major exceptions. for one, the excitement around @solana among researchers is undeniable: it's crushingly good tech, massively improved over the bear market and liberated from the stain of sbf to the auspices of @aeyakovenko, one of the best founders in the space. there's lots of reasons you might fud solana, but let's be real, low throughput/tps is not one. the actual major challenges for solana are a) the network effects of the EVM and b) matching the world championship braintrust of the @drakefjustin and @TimBeiko types working in ethereum. both are steep indeed. but ultimately, dismissing solana at this point is not so different—as a few people put it—from dismissing ethereum in the heyday of bitcoin dominance around 2017. both camps are well positioned to win, solana for fast composability and ethereum for app-chain sovereignty, and that's why dismissing one can only be done at your own peril. all of that also explains the excitement around that other L1, still unlaunched. in many ways, @monad_xyz represents the best of solana's parallelizable execution with ethereum's network effects of the evm. liquidity aggregation, economic security, and, yes, braintrust will be its own challenges, as they are for any L1. but... but... well, i'll just say as a full disclosure that i turned down angeling in @monad_xyz last year because i thought it would be like any other L1. it's already clear enough now that i was wrong. it's not. (i am also personally excited by @berachain, an EVM-cosmos chain, but my major complaint about devconnect is that it just didn't have enough devs in cheap bear costumes as it should have.) 2. mev centralization is the number one issue facing ethereum right now, everyone knows it, and nobody wants to talk about it, because—unlike with governance centralization—there's very, very little we can do. frankly, all of us building in ethereum need to be very worried not only about the technical risks of centralization in ethereum (extending to mev, single sequencers, liquidity on centralized exchanges, and 5-person L2 multisigs), but the reputational risk in incentivizing a new wave of devs to build elsewhere. see point #1. 3. lest any of that sound negative towards ethereum, let's be honest: ethereum is the easiest, most trusted, most interoperable way to build onchain, and those advantages continuously get stronger, especially as ethereum mainnet itself looks increasingly to be the *receipt layer* of the internet, where all other services and chains leave hashes attesting to their transactions. 4. mpc (multiparty computation) is in a kind of unsexy no-mans-land right now between account abstraction on one side (for automating transactions through permissionless signing) and zk on the other (for privacy and encryption). in istanbul, there was at least one zk event everyday, usually more, and not a single one for mpc. and then, well, there is also another issue with mpc as well right now: you can divide a key into multiparty shares, but unless you can distribute these keys on a decentralized network, you still face massive centralization risks. but here's the thing. AA is hell for us multichain builders, with its different implementations for different chains. zk itself actually *needs* mpc for full privacy, as @SmartCryptology explained recently on @zeroknowledgefm—they go hand-in-hand. and all eyes are on @LitProtocol right now to launch a distributed keyshare network. and that's only a part of of why mpc is about to have a major moment: for any kind of private encryption or onchain automation without the UX pains of signing and approving every transaction, mpc is the way (indeed, @usecapsule launched one during devconnect). and it is, yes, a key part of the future of zk. 5. one major missing opportunity in crypto: using zk-privacy to let users opt into sharing their data with advertisers, platforms, social networks, etc, in exchange for revenue-sharing and an improved social feed. this is one of those exclusive opportunities from building on financial rails with zkps, but also one that would make users *much* more comfortable, emotionally and financially, in interacting onchain. overall we need to stop thinking that the point of internet privacy is just privacy for its own sake—and recognize the real opportunity is monetizing our data as its rightful owners. 6. another major missing opportunity in crypto: a reputation protocol built as an analytics platform to support current nft-badging systems. we're about to face a flood of social attestations in the form of votes, submissions, bets, etc—all of which any community should be able to analyze easily to determine access, rewards, governance power, etc. instead of just thinking of nfts as badges, we can also think of *any social transaction onchain* as a badge of sort... and one which might entitle you to earn role-based nfts on a protocol like @hatsprotocol in turn. most importantly, this analytics platform would help us solve the dominant chicken-egg in social reputation right now: nobody can leverage reputation meaningfully, so nobody is incentivized to develop reputation for it to be leveraged. we need good data tools to incentivize people to generate that data in the first place. i'm looking at @bellosights 7. most web3 apps are worst than web2 apps because they're still being built offchain to try to harvest user's data—matching the beloved monetization models of web2 with the beloved UI/UX of web3. 8. finally, even within crypto, very few people believe that the future of social, gaming, and reputation is onchain. i am one of them, and i spent a good part of a week pitching chains to use their own chains. my pitch was a five-parter: a. enabling users to build onchain reputation not only lets these users leverage their activity for access and airdrops but incentivizes them to engage in the first place to earn these b. anyone building onchain turns their platform into a protocol that anyone also can build on top of, kind of like a permissionless app store for plugins: actions on one service can trigger actions on another, driving more use cases and users (h/t @seanmc_eth) c. by extension, it's easier to build businesses than ever onchain—because you can just build a module on top of a protocol that supports it while drawing its users and sharing its revenue. at @jokerace_xyz alone, some of the businesses people could build on us include gamified hackathons, citizens journalism bounty platforms, live game shows, a decentralized product hunt, and gaming communities to cocreate characters. all are monetizable on top of us in a way they couldn't be offchain in web2. d. the biggest barrier to doing anything onchain right now is just the ux pain of bridging over liquidity—so any service that incentivizes users to do so is a boon to every other app built on that chain as well e. most importantly, when you build on the financial rails of blockchains, you not only avoid credit card and app store fees but can *directly monetize any action* by topping off gas fees and even sharing revenue with users as an incentive mechanism (h/t @pet3rpan_) this was, for the most part, an effective pitch. and it is, for me, the best bull case i can personally make for the future of crypto. now my job is getting others to agree. 9. turkey is grappling with 60% annual inflation, and it's no surprise to see crypto shops along the street as a result—in the way they're simply not in the US. in all our whale-centric ponzi-bootstrapped euphoria right now, a country like turkey is a reminder of how big the stakes are for building money backed by global consensus rather than state violence. istanbul is also, for that matter, one of the most vibrant, multicultural (and yes, safe) cities in the world, so i want to make a personal plea: please, more conferences in cities like istanbul that have clear uses for this tech, rich cultural history, and most importantly, tons and tons of cats.

Front ends are just writing assistants. You want to freely associate and communicate with your peers by publishing publicly and provably to the blockchain, but remembering the format and doing the math is hard, so you use a "front end" to assist you with your communication. You verify that the "front end" helped you correctly when you hit that metam@sk approval screen where it shows you what you will be communicating exactly. Thus in the end, what you freely speak to the public via the blockchain is all that matters, and your "front end" and "wallet" are just speech assistants, like a word processor. Why does this matter? Because you have many different paths that end up in the same result of that same speech. Your word processor like speech assistant code could be run on your device by an IPFS or zip file, or compiled yourself from source from gitlab, or from someone else's computer on the net that already did the same. In the end, your speech is all that matters, and which code repository generated the binary that you're running on your device to assist you doesn't really matter much. Unless it's evil. Then it matters a lot. Because maybe when you inspect your speech, you don't notice the evil. Thus, how do you know what you're running is what you think you're running. Welcome to the magic of hashes sir. Hashes are the core driving principle behind all blockchains. Period. A hash is a function that takes a lot of data and turns it into a very small amount of data, a tag if you will. So that you can tag things and know what they are, quickly. And if any little thing changes at all in the thing tagged, the tag would change massively. This way software releases have tags (hashes) and you know what code you're running, because you can inspect the hash before you run it. So it doesn't matter where in the world you downloaded something from, as long as the hash matches what you know it should, then you know it's safe to run. Enter IPFS. What's that you say? It's an innovative way of storing data. Instead of giving files names, and organizing files by their names, as you do on your personal devices, you instead just hash all the files, and organize them by their hashes. This does a few very cool things. 1. Everyone really knows what they're really downloading, because you can fake file names but you can't fake file hashes. 2. Deduplication. You know what files are dupes, instantly, because their hashes match. 3. Security. No one can pull the old switcheroo on you and replace what was once safe with something evil, because the hash would change. So IPFS is pretty great, in that, when you browse to a file hash, you know exactly what you're getting. Because you're browsing to a hash, and a hash is the purest form of knowing what've you have actually got. You can run IPFS natively in some browsers, or you can use an extension in chrome. Or you can use other people websites "gateway", but that's not as secure, because they could change the site's code. Time for some more education. Developers edit text for a living. And they edit that text alongside thousands of other developers, and all that text has to get merged and deleted and cut and extended and rolled back, you name it. And how do they do all that? Using VCS "Version control system" such as GIT. And how does GIT keep track? Hashes. And what is every block in a blockchain? Hashes. Hashes are cool. They've even got something called DHT, a "Distributed Hash Table" that drives Bittorrent, and other things. There's lots of different hash functions and what makes them better is when they're fast to run, and don't have collisions. A collision is where two different files generate the same hash, which they shouldn’t. As always your screen must trust the GPU, the GPU must trust the CPU , the CPU must trust the hard drive, the hard drive must trust its firmware, and then there's the OS, etc, etc. There's always trust, the trick is to replace the trust with proof as much as you can, and that's what hashes do. And it works, because the vast majority of cryptocurrency users are unhacked, regardless of skill level. And let's be serious, there's some unskilled folks out there. TLDR; Wallets and front ends are just word processors that help you speak publicly (publish). Hashing them lets you know exactly what code your running. IPFS is based on hashes.

WTF is mempool sniping? Here is everything you need to know: This morning Ordinals entered a new era of PvP warfare in the mempool (otherwise known as MEV on Ethereum) when a group of sophisticated botters picked off many of the OrdiBots mints from the people who thought they had minted them. Let's break down what happened and what this means going forward. Ordinals inscriptions are traded using PSBT swaps (partially signed Bitcoin transactions). The way it works is the seller signs an off-chain PSBT that states that anybody can complete the swap as long as X amount of BTC is sent to the seller's address. A marketplace guards this off-chain PSBT until a buyer comes along and signs the other half at which point the transaction is broadcasted to the Bitcoin network. The swap transaction now sits in the mempool waiting for a miner to confirm it but because Bitcoin blocks are mined ~10 minutes apart it will likely sit there for a long time. During this waiting period, anybody can retrieve a PSBT from the mempool, sign it themselves, and submit their version back into the mempool but with a higher fee so that it will be confirmed first. This front-running technique is known as "mempool sniping" and it is how many of the PSBT mints for OrdiBots were picked off this morning. The OrdiBots mint was likely the tip of the iceberg. I expect tooling to come online in the next several weeks that will allow anyone to go to a website and with a few clicks snipe inscription purchases from the mempool. This means that if you purchase an inscription on an Ordinals marketplace or are minting a hot Ordinals drop, you aren't guaranteed to receive it. If somebody snipes your purchase from the mempool you will be refunded the BTC you paid but you also won't receive the inscription. But let's take things a step further. It is also likely that these tools will allow you to front-run the actual inscribing part as well which could be very profitable in first-is-first style metaprotocols. For example, you could front-run someone who is deploying a BRC-20 token by registering the ticker first, or in a first-is-first byte-perfect collection mint you could inscribe the same image as someone else but pay just a 1 sat higher fee in order to be first. Lastly, if you throw into the mix that in certain high-value situations a miner could theoretically kick everyone else's transactions out of the block and insert their own, you could see how things could get messy very quickly. The is called selfish mining. Just as there will be tools for sniping other people's transactions I expect there to be tools for protecting your own transactions as well. Other chains like Ethereum have dealt with MEV/frontrunning for years, but it is a new concept on Bitcoin, so we will need to wake up to this reality and get much more sophisticated very quickly. The best outcome here is that we create easy to use mempool sniping and monitoring tools that everyone has access to in order to prevent a scenario where a select few are able to prey on the masses.

Most of the criticisms I've seen center on the idea that Solana has lower fees and therefore will not flip Ethereum which is securing more value and has higher fee extraction. Higher fees = higher net present value of network...where is the fault in that logic? Utility, not scarcity, drives network value. Imagine thinking dial-up internet was better than broadband because it costs more. Cheaper and faster broadband internet opened up a vast number of use cases and created much more value in the aggregate (less value flowed to extractive network providers and more to apps). When I say Solana can flip Ethereum I am looking at the aggregate ecosystem. My thesis is that blockchains are the settlement layer of the internet. Therefore the question becomes: which blockchain can facilitate most of that flow in a cost-efficient and scaleable manner? It's not mutually exclusive. I think Solana's integrated design is more elegant than a more fragmented L1/L2 environment - that's most important in DeFi but less so in apps that don't require atomic composability. I also think cross-chain integration and interoperability will improve vastly so this debate may be short lived. Finally, dynamic and cheaper fee markets make blockchains more efficient. They open up a real possibility to move much more transfers on-chain at scale (DeFi, gaming, NFTs, and other consumer applications). So I think blockchains that do this have a higher probability of processing much more value on-chain. Higher fees extracted today is myopic. Only a few hobbyists were willing to pay for dial-up. Cheaper internet was necessary for mainstream adoption. The better discussion to be had is on value extraction (where and in what proportion at the different layers of the stack) when most of the world's transfers of value run on blockchains.

Today I'd like to share a project I worked on in the past 1-2 months👇 Reth Crawler Reth Crawler is a dedicated tool for the Ethereum execution layer, having successfully mapped approximately 30,000 nodes in just 10 days. It leverages the Reth P2P stack for discovering nodes and uses Ethereum wire network protocols for connecting with them. This approach facilitates continuous scanning of the network, allowing for the discovery and connection to new nodes. The crawler operates with a two-database system. The primary database, integral to the backend, records details from each new node connection. Then, at five-minute intervals, a secondary database updates itself with information from the primary database. This secondary database is the one that powers the RESTful API, providing up-to-date data to the frontend. Reth Crawler offers valuable insights into the Ethereum network's structure, answering important questions such as: - The most commonly used Ethereum clients and the significance of client diversity. - Geographic distribution of the clients. - Preferred operating systems and programming languages among clients. - Status of nodes in terms of synchronization with the latest blockchain block. - (Work in Progress) Breakdown of nodes into categories like archive, full, or pruned. - The most used ISP by these nodes. Bitcoin has steadily outperformed Ethereum over the past 16 months. A core reason for this outperformance has been the optimism for a spot #Bitcoin ETF approval. Here's why the time may finally be coming for ETH to outperform 👇🏼 As we continue to approach the final deadline for the SEC to approve or deny a spot Bitcoin ETF, we have seen a clear bullish trend for BTC fueled by institutional positioning. This is clearly evident from the increase in CME BTC futures open interest which has grown from $1.9 billion in mid-October to $4.9 billion now. Further evidence of institutional positioning for an approval is the CME BTC futures annualized basis steadily increasing from 4.5% in early September to 16.5% now. Bloomberg’s ETF analysts have shared that the most likely window of time for a final SEC decision is from January 8-10. This was fairly widely expected due to expectations for Gensler to take as long as possible before a potential approval. However, in spite of those expectations, institutions and the rest of us have been positioning months in advance in order to take advantage of the increasing optimism and buying pressure the closer we get to that potential approval. This brings us to why it may be time to start paying attention to Ethereum, while the majority of people are still focused on the Bitcoin ETF decision. If a spot BTC ETF is approved in early January as is expected, then it is highly likely that a spot ETH ETF will be approved soon afterwards. This is due to the legal arguments being used to gain a spot BTC ETF approval. Essentially, the argument is that the SEC approved BTC futures ETFs, and because BTC futures are materially similar to spot BTC, the SEC should also approve spot BTC ETFs. This argument is what won Grayscale their appeal against the SEC to force them to reevaluate their previous denial to convert gBTC into a spot BTC ETF. If this argument works and an approval is given for spot BTC ETFs, then the exact same argument would be able to be used for spot ETH ETFs, as the SEC has already approved ETH futures ETFs. The tradfi giants already know this, which is why BlackRock, Fidelity, VanEck and others already filed their spot ETH ETF applications. The first final deadline for a spot ETH ETF decision is currently 23 May 2024 for VanEck’s application. Of course, a decision can be made before this final deadline but as we have seen with the spot BTC ETF process, the SEC is in no hurry to approve new crypto investment products. There is already some evidence that institutions may be starting to position for a spot ETH ETF narrative as open interest for CME ETH futures is up ~61% since the start of November and CME ETH futures annualized basis has increased from 1.5% in mid-October to 14.5% now. The Grayscale ETHe trust discount has also been shrinking, reaching -15% now after being as large as -56% in June. Finally, it is worth noting that ETH is still down -40% against Bitcoin from its previous bull market highs. However, the ETH/BTC chart does appear to potentially be nearing a bottom which would provide a nice confluence with the emergence of a narrative around rotating from BTC to ETH as the focus begins to shift towards a potential spot ETH ETF approval. A great crypto thesis: @Solana will disrupt @Apple, @Samsung, @google and cloud service providers @Microsoft and @amazon Yes, that’s right. I’m not talking about Ethereum, Polygon, Cardano, Avalanche, Hedera, or any other chain. And no, I’m not talking about the Saga phone. I’m talking about the world of software applications. I think Solana in particular will be the crypto winner in this domain by a wide margin. Let’s talk about why… The application layer Imagine you buy a new phone. It doesn’t matter which brand, but imagine that this phone costs you $1000, and it’s better than an iPhone. Way better. It’s loaded up with all the apps you expect, but they are better than the Apple equivalents. The calendar/to-do apps are all built by third parties, so you can pick which ones you like the most, but they all integrate seamlessly together. They can share your data between them. Want to switch to a new calendar app? Just download it, and you don’t even need to migrate your data to the new app. It’s already there when you open the app. Now imagine you open your navigation app, and all those calendar events are loaded into it, and it offers a screen that tells you the estimated commute times for each event location. No app integrations necessary. Not only that, but you can open a random restaurant recommendation app, and an AI model will look at your travel patterns, grocery preferences, and pre-existing eating habits, and automatically recommend 10 new restaurants that you’re going to love. But you’re feeling more adventurous, and you speak to it, saying, “I was actually thinking about trying out Himalayan food, preferably not too expensive” and it produces a nice (probably small) list of options. You say, “schedule a date with my wife for tomorrow at that second one on the list,” and it creates a calendar event, invites your wife (who uses a totally different calendar app), and makes the reservation for you. Now imagine that all of this happens without any centralized entity collecting your personal data. It’s all encrypted and it all lives on the Solana blockchain. Not only that, but all the apps are super cheap and usually free. The only catch is that you spend about $3/month on SOL that you need in order to use these apps. How is this possible? Well, the entire point of blockchains is to have a globally shared state that can be accessed by anyone at any time. Imagine if all the Web2 tech companies shared a single database and could integrate all their apps together to give you a seamless user experience across all of them. Solana enables that. With this type of system, we don’t need those big tech companies collecting “platform rent.” Individual companies lose their network effect when the network is global, permissionless, and open-source. Now the companies building applications will need to focus less on building a huge moat of personal data capture & exclusive “walled gardens” of applications, and will instead focus more on delivering great user experiences. They won’t be able to rest on their laurels because they have all their users locked in. Users can’t be locked in if their data is freely available to competing apps. The friction of switching to a new app becomes nonexistent. “Ethereum gas prices are too high and it’s slow.” Ethereum L1: -Ethereum (High Gas Fees) Ethereum L2: -Optimism (cheap) -Arbitrum (cheap) -Polygon (cheap) -Base (cheap) -zkSync (cheap) -ImmutableX (literally zero) -Linea (cheap) -Scroll (cheap) Ethereum might’ve been just the L1 in the past but has since evolved and expanded into a network of networks. All of these L2’s use ETH for gas. All of these L2’s settle on Ethereum the L1. All of these L2’s burn ETH and produce revenue for Ethereum. You can hate on Ethereum all you want, but it’s false to claim Ethereum has high gas costs or is too slow. One PIECE of Ethereum has high gas costs and is slower. However that piece isn’t meant to be used by retail. It’s a settlement layer for L2 and a place for large transactions that require the highest level of trust and security. Retail activity has been moving to L2’s all throughout the bear market. Which has low fees and high transaction speeds. The L1 will likely always retain the highest security and the L2’s will experiment with different levels of security, decentralization, specializations and more. Some are even building the SVM, MOVE, fully private chains, etc on Ethereum. It’s a free and open market ripe with experimentation and that’s the point! As a user you can choose which one aligns with your values, needs and level of security you’re comfortable with. Now some like to point out that “bridging is a bad UX and you’re fracturing the liquidity.” You’re assuming that these networks won’t find a way to become interoperable. However we have Chainlink’s CCIP, intents based bridges and dex’s, Polygons unified liquidity using zk and a ton of other solutions to this issue that are primed to be ready to deploy THIS cycle. If interoperability is solved, and moving between these chains is as if it’s all one single chain, then a world of specialized chains is the future. At that point restaking, L2’s, app chains, modularity all make a lot of sense. And Ethereum as a network of networks vs a single shared state also makes a lot of sense.

End of year thoughts on Bitcoin. Bitcoin’s core idea is finiteness. No other blockchain really gets this, Ethereum claims it is “sound money” which is a joke. It’s entire issuance schedule was updated just two years ago, and a burn mechanism was bolted on to make it appear “deflationary” Solana did 5 rounds of private sales, including a validator sale, and several strategic sales. On the way, the team got 20% of the tokens, for free. This is not the kind of chain that could ever qualify as money. There will only ever be 21 million Bitcoin. No matter what country is the leading the world, no matter what the deficit is or interest rates are, no matter who is in power, and what wars are being fought, the fundamental idea of Bitcoin is this: exactly 21 million units. YapStones worked because of a similar finiteness. For hundreds of years, there were a maximum of 10,000 stones (roughly) on Yap Island. No other stones could be created, because there was no natural limestone on the island. So, when transferring an asset, a verbal transfer of Yap Stone ownership was made. I spent 7 years of my life deeply immersed in mathematics. To me, Bitcoin is what we call a “canonical form” of proof of work. Everything else can be reduced to it. As Adam Back noted, you can tinker with it, but you can't improve it. Ethereum on the other hand, has been tinkered with now for 8 years. That is NOT A GOOD THING. People keep saying "keep on Bulding" in Blockchain, but great results in math do not need tinkering with. Solana is again being tinkered with with some kind of new "firedancer" protocol. This is fine for a product, not for money. I can't see people using SOL tokens 50 years from now. Or ETH. But they will be using Bitcoin. Eventually, we will as a planet be thinking in units of Bitcoin. It's a mathematical certainty, and it really has nothing to do with any of the "add ons" to Bitcoin, or any competing chain. It's just the fundamental mathematical idea that will continue working. Our lives are finite, and the goal is not to die with the most Bitcoin, but to use it over the course of your life to enjoy it to the maximum. If you truly understand this, you are incredibly fortunate -- I'm convinced it's like really getting Amazon or Microsoft at the very begining of these companies. It will be enough to be early. Lets celebrate this amazing invention, and here's to an amazing 2024!

Interoperability: Cardano is not just about its own ecosystem. Its pursuit of becoming a "blockchain of blockchains" means better connectivity with other systems in the future. I see a lot of confusion going around about Farcaster, what is it, what is Warpcast, etc. Here's a quick post explaining: In their own words: Farcaster is a sufficiently decentralized social network built on Ethereum. Users can create profiles, post short messages or "casts", follow others and organize into communities. It is a public social network similar in design to Twitter and Reddit. Since Farcaster is public and decentralized, anyone can build an app to read and write data. Users own their accounts and relationships with other users and are free to move between different apps. Farcaster is the underlying network, on top of which anyone can (and many people have) build apps with which to interact with the protocol Warpcast is the most popular app. It's basically a Twitter/X clone, with a few tweaks [improvements imo]. You can set up an account by going to warpcast[dot]com. There's a small yearly fee required in order to prevent against bots, but that's currently being waved in about 15-20 countries. Another way to engage with Farcaster is via Flink (flink[dot]fyi). This is a reddit-style interface (I really recommend trying it, it's amazing). The same content, same accounts, just engaged with in an entirely new format. That's the beauty of Farcaster. Warpcast actually went "down" yesterday. The app was overwhelmed, and people couldn't log in. But FARCASTER did not go down. The underlying protocol worked just find, and other apps (such as Flink, or Supercast) kept running - so people were able to continue to engage with their content and others just fine. The beauty of decentralization. DeSo (Decentralized Social) has been spoken about a lot over the last few years, and got a tonne of attention last year with Friend Tech. I'm a huge believer in DeSo and think it is the future, in no small part because it is significantly better for the end user (not to mention for developers). A big problem in the past with all previous DeSo attempts has been the hyper financialization and ponzification of it all. Farcaster has no native token, there is no ponzi, it is just a good product, built by great developers, and used by great developers. I really recommend people actually try it out. Spend an hour or two on it. There's SO MUCH cool stuff happening there, and it's rapidly gaining momentum. Is it a Twitter/X killer? Probably not. Is it a Reddit killer? Probably not. Is it a Facebook killer? Probably not. Does it need to be? Probably not. I used to think in order for a new social network to survive/win, it needed to "dethrone" an incumbent. I no longer think that is true -- if it is slowly gaining users, over time, it can grow into it's own social network in it's own right. I don't think any of the existing social networks are likely to disappear or become irrelevant any time soon. But I don't think they need to, in order for Farcaster to be a success. And, personally, I think it is in the best interests of the world for Farcaster to succeed. Give it a go.

#Ethereum I'm here to protect you from scams again. Scammers want to trick you into sending to their scam addresses. Here's one you might not have seen yet. 1. Create a new address with the same starting and ending characters as a real address that you've sent to. 2. Make a fake transaction so that etherscan shows as thought you actually sent to their fake address before. They copy the last send's value, and name of token (but it's a fake token, so usually grayed out with no logo showing in etherscan.) 3. Do this to lots of addresses and wait for people to fall for it. Why does this trick work? Because people trust what etherscan showed them, instead of using their own history stored locally. Because they didn't use a test transaction and confirm with the other party, or yourself, whatever might see the real balance of the real token at the real address. Because showing just the starting and ending characters of an address is basically harmful if scammers can just create addresses of their own with the same start and end and only the middle characters are different. This is where devs can do better, by showing the start, end and middle. Basically, the idea of "fingerprint." Being used to make more human identifiable one long string from a different long string has been around a long time. For example, when you click the lock certificate and inspect an SSL security certificate. A simple fix would be to show some middle characters for now as well.

Releasing the Type-1 upgrade to the zkEVM prover, the next generation of Polygon’s proving tech. It can generate proofs for any EVM chain—sidechain, optimistic rollup, even Ethereum itself. When proving Ethereum mainnet blocks, avg per-transaction costs are $0.002 - $0.003. Developed with @Toposware, the Type 1 is open source and available today. Together with the AggLayer, the Type 1 prover will allow EVM chains to upgrade to ZK and access the shared state, liquidity, and user-base of the Polygon ecosystem. What makes it a Type 1? Ethereum equivalence. The Type 1 prover preserves all of Ethereum’s execution logic. In practice, this means that any EVM chain can become a ZK Layer 2, without having to fork or make modifications. We joke that it’s “BTC Denver” now, but the reality is that Bitcoin has been MIA since 2017, and devs in the ETH ecosystem (later in Solana and others) carried the flag. - The Bitcoin renaissance is real. More than 1,000 people registered for the Bitcoin L2 event (not organized by us), and the energy and dev momentum there was palpable. I was trying to help create Bitcoin L2s as a category before. Now, it feels like no one can stop Bitcoin L2s from emerging even if they tried. - There were a few rotten tomatoes (ETH maxis) who left a bad taste on smaller incidents, but overall the community and vibe were super friendly, open to Bitcoin, and builder-focused. I enjoyed my time a lot, made new connections and learned new things from devs in the trenches. - BitVM is a game changer. I haven’t met a Bitcoin L2 yet that doesn’t want to help support it (Stacks ecosystem included), and we should expect rapid R&D and advancement in BitVM-based L1 to L2 bridges with minimal trust. - Bitcoin L2 and DeFi apps on Bitcoin L2 are attracting significant capital now. I got so many pings from investors to help connect with new founders. DM me. I want to be helpful and can add you to Telegram groups where we share early-stage Bitcoin L2 deal flow. - Stacks ecosystem continues to be a leader in this category. People come up to me and say sweet things like “You guys believed when no one did”. “You kept building when there was no light at the end of the tunnel.” I appreciate all these comments. Looking back, I think we held an irrational belief that all successful experiments in crypto will eventually come to Bitcoin. It took a few years longer than we expected, but we survived and are now emerging as stronger than ever to make it happen. - A strong sense I got from new L2 projects and new devs building apps is that we all want to grow the pie for everyone. That’d be my strong preference as well. Bitcoin L2s right now are too small a category for needless completion and in-fighting. We are all here to grow the BTC economy. We all win if Bitcoin wins. Let’s focus on that. In summary, I am leaving Denver more bullish than ever on BTC (which is all my savings for 11 years now) and bullish on Bitcoin L2s and builder culture. It’s time to build on Bitcoin 🟧

Why build an Ethereum L2? ——— Some argue that “Ethereum is a great settlement layer and that’s why L2s should settle there. “ ——— Our theory (not financial advice): Anyone who wants to use and transact with ETH, the asset, needs to settle on Ethereum, which is the final ledger of record of ETH. The less trust assumptions that are imposed in this settlement process, the better it is. Hence chains that want to use ETH become L2s and settle on Ethereum. Other chains that want to interoperate trustlessly with existing Ethereum L2s now have to build as an Ethereum L2 as well. This gives rise to a “trustless composability” network effect. The more the net L2 state built, the more other L2s want to cohabit, the larger the inhabitable surface area of ETH becomes. If the inhabitable throughput can be made infinite, all chains can be built and interoperate on a common substrate. If DA throughput goes to infinity, even if the fees go to zero, it is extremely beneficial to the Ethereum ecosystem, and I would say the right outcome for the ecosystem. The many people reasoning about “composability” network effects obsessed about atomic composition. We can split composability mechanisms in two dimensions: a) timescale: atomic execution, atomic inclusion, asynchronous, b) trust: trust-an-intermediate-zone, trust-only-sending-and-receiving-zones, trustless (or trust-minimized). The L2 architecture is asynchronous and trustless. It does not optimize for maximizing atomic composition bandwidth, but the total trustless composition throughout. Given blockchains are trust machines, this is the most important dimension. There are many excellent out of protocol ways to do faster composition. Our goal @eigenlayer is to build humanity’s coordination zone with infinite coordination bandwidth and universal convergence. The last property is very important - if we want to build global systems of coordination, all parties should converge on a system that can trustlessly interoperate without divergence - this is not possible when “interoperating across different chains” which can diverge. We see @ethereum as the highest possibility candidate for this universal convergence. Hence @eigenlayer is built on @ethereum, the same reason why chains want to become Ethereum L2s.
